Q: How to write a video file using Moviepy A:

The issue you are running into may be caused by due to few mismatched data types and parameters between librosa and moviepy.

Main things causing this problem can be due to:

  1. Array Shape: librosa outputs a 1-Dimensional array, but moviepy's AudioArrayClip strictly requires a 2-Dimensional [tag:numpy array] shaped as (samples, channels). Your list comprehension was a good guess, but numpy.reshape is the standard way to fix this.

  2. Audio Sample Rate vs. Video FPS: You passed fps = new_vid.fps to the audio clip. Video FPS is usually around 24 or 30, while audio sample rate (sr) is usually 22050 or 44100. Giving the audio clip the video's FPS will completely break the audio playback. So it needs sr.

  3. Data Types (Clipping): librosa.load returns audio as floating-point numbers between -1.0 and 1.0. Generating noise with a standard deviation of 1 and converting everything to int64 will cause massive audio distortion. You should keep the audio as floats and scale down the noise.

Here's the one of the ways that you can modify this code,

# (Previous code up to creating the noise)....

# 1. Create startle burst (Scaled down amplitude to 0.5 so it doesn't clip)
noise = np.random.normal(0, 0.5, len(burst_window)) 

# 2. Insert the noise into the original audio (keeping it as floats)
audio[start_point_samp : start_point_samp + burst_samp] = audio[start_point_samp : start_point_samp + burst_samp] + noise

librosa.display.waveplot(audio, sr=sr) 
sd.play(audio, sr) 

# 3. Reshape the 1D librosa array into a 2D numpy array (N, 1) for mono
# This replaces the slow list comprehension
audio_2d = np.reshape(audio, (-1, 1))

# (Note: if you need stereo, you would use: audio_2d = np.vstack((audio, audio)).T)

# 4. Create the AudioArrayClip
# Important: Use the audio sample rate (sr), NOT the video fps
new_audio_clip = AudioArrayClip(audio_2d, fps=sr)

# 5. Set the new audio to the video clip
new_vid = vid.set_audio(new_audio_clip)

# 6. Write the final video file
# It is highly recommended to explicitly pass the audio_fps here as well
new_vid.write_videofile('37vids_balanced_noise/Baby_Babble.mp4', audio_fps=sr)

Hope this will resolve your issue.

Q: Fixing date and time column format in R A:

It sounds like there was some mis-parsing upstream of your current data. It'd be best to fix this upstream. If you can't, you could use:

library(tidyverse)
df |>
  mutate(date2 = str_sub(date, start = 3) |> mdy_hm(),
         date_fmt = format(date2, "%m-%d-%Y %H:%M")) |>
  tibble() # to show data types in header

date2 strips the leading (and misleading!) first two digits from the month data, and reinterprets the resulting string assuming it represents data in MDY H:M order. This results in a POSIXct datetime ("ddtm") column that you can calculate on. If you want to see that represented in mdy order (but no longer directly calculatable), you can use format to make text ("chr") with that ordering.

# A tibble: 13 × 3
   date             date2               date_fmt        
   <chr>            <dttm>              <chr>

Q: How to optimize $O(N)$ insertion time in a custom Java Singly Linked List used as a Priority Queue? A:

Your insertWithPriority is linear with List-size, because you iterate the list. Therefore, inserting N elements can be expected to be quadratic, and that is exactly what you measure. To optimize this code, you have to get the complexity of insertWithPriority down. Iteration of the whole list is not an option. So how can you go about this?

You want to maintain a sorted list by inserting a new element into the right position. If you use a linked list, insertion itself is O(1) but you can only find the right position by O(N) iteration. If you use an array-based list, you can O(logN) find the right index to insert the element using binary search, but the actual insertion is O(N), so that will not do. Neither of these simple datastructures can provide you with a sublinear insert operation.

There are a variety of tree-based datastructures that will allow you to have O(logN) insertions while maintaining order. A simple binary tree comes to mind, though that is not a good datastructure both in practice and in theory. B-Trees, Red-Black-Trees and Skip-lists are some examples of advancements on the binary tree idea. You will have to use one of those if you want to maintain an ordered list. With one of those, you will get O(NlogN) runtime for your benchmarks.

But the real trick of implementing a priority-queue is understanding that you do not need to maintain a fully sorted list at all times. It is sufficient for a queue to support only the following operations in addition to insert:

head - get the first element
pop - remove the first element

All three of those operations are sublinear on a datastructure called "Heap" or "Priority Queue". head is O(1), pop and insert are O(logN). This datastructure is explained in depth elsewhere, so I will only give the gist here: The "Heap" is a tree with the invariant that parent-nodes hold bigger values than the children.
